problem: Existing VLN agents only interpret instructions into actions ("dumb" wayfinders), and instruction-generation speakers are separate models, so no single agent can both follow and generate navigation instructions or explain its behavior.
motivation: Two-way language communication completes the human-robot loop (progress reports, guiding humans, building trust) and makes agents more explainable. Instruction following and generation are dual tasks whose shared visual-linguistic knowledge could be exploited in one model, but prior work trains them separately.
key_idea: A single Transformer with two shared unimodal encoders (route, language) and two task-specific multimodal decoders (route decoder for action prediction, language decoder for instruction generation), jointly trained on both tasks during pretraining and fine-tuning.
insight: Joint training on both tasks helps both: the ablation on R2R val-unseen shows joint pretraining plus fine-tuning (row 8: SR 67.9, SPL 61.6, SPICE 0.226) beats single-task fine-tuning after joint pretraining (row 6: SR 65.7; row 7: SPICE 0.223) and single-task pretraining (row 4: SR 61.3). Generation-based pretraining thus transfers to grounding. The multi-task model has 143M parameters versus 220M for two separate models. The generated descriptions give post-hoc behavior explanations that can reveal failure modes.
method: Route Encoder E^r: tokenizes each step's panorama (36 views) and action; compresses the panorama into an action-attentive route state r_t = a_t + cross_att(a_t, O_t), then applies self-attention over the history (plus current panorama tokens when following); 1 layer
Language Encoder E^l: 9-layer Transformer encoder over the instruction (following) or previously generated words (generation, causal mask)
Route Decoder D^r: 4 blocks of cross-attention (route/observation attend to instruction) plus self-attention; outputs a softmax over K navigable views plus STOP
Language Decoder D^l: 4 blocks of cross-attention (words attend to route) plus causal self-attention; autoregressive word distribution over the vocabulary

Joint training: language-modeling loss L^g (next-word NLL, teacher forcing) plus action NLL L^f, sampled per mini-batch (IG:IF:ITM=4:1:2 in pretraining, IG:IF=2:5 in fine-tuning); pretrained on PREVALENT (104K R2R plus 6482K synthetic pairs); fine-tuned with IL+RL (A3C)
Variants: Lana_mt (joint fine-tuning, one model) vs Lana_st (joint pretraining, per-task fine-tuning)

setting.backbone: Lana Transformer (route encoder, language encoder, two decoders; d=768), trained from scratch
setting.training_data: PREVALENT pretraining (104K R2R + 6482K synthetic instruction-route pairs), then fine-tuning on R2R / R4R / REVERIE with IL+RL; optional DUET-augmented REVERIE data
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views) with heading/elevation orientation features; object features on REVERIE

results: Lana_mt reaches R2R val-unseen SR 68 / SPL 62, above HAMT (65/59) and HOP (64/57), and R4R CLS 59.7. On instruction generation, both variants beat CCC-speaker on every SPICE setting (R2R val-unseen SPICE 0.226 vs 0.214). In the user study, humans prefer Lana to CCC (63.4% vs 36.6%) and to BT-Speaker (75.1% vs 24.9%), but still prefer human-written instructions (69.3% vs 30.7%).
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation; real-robot deployment and collision safety are untested
Generated descriptions are post-hoc explanations and do not exactly reflect the agent's inner decision process; they lag behind human-written instructions
Discrete nav-graph setting only; pretraining relies on synthetic data from a speaker trained on R2R
